health-tech-41092313cf.fulltext:
From Scale to Systems: Mapping India’s Digital Health Progress Across States, 2026
India’s digital health transformation is entering a more consequential phase in 2026. Over the past few years, the country has built a large digital foundation through the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), creating digital identities for citizens, registries for healthcare facilities and professionals, and the infrastructure needed to support interoperable and consent-based exchange of health information.
The scale is now substantial. As of July 20, 2026, India had created 94.87 crore Ayushman Bharat Health Accounts (ABHAs), while the Health Facility Registry (HFR) had 5.36 lakh registered facilities and the Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR) had 10.09 lakh registered professionals. By July 2026, more than 100 crore health records had been linked with ABHAs, marking another major milestone for the country's digital health ecosystem.
Yet national numbers tell only part of the story. India's digital health transformation is increasingly being shaped by what individual states are doing with this infrastructure. The state-level picture reveals different pathways to digital-health maturity. Uttar Pradesh is driving absolute scale, Andhra Pradesh is demonstrating very high population-level ABHA saturation, Bihar has emerged as the leading state for Scan and Register digital OPD registrations, while Rajasthan and Gujarat demonstrate how existing state digital-health platforms can connect with the national ABDM architecture.
Tamil Nadu is extending ABDM integration into health insurance, Karnataka is using digital systems to support referrals, while Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh illustrate why population-adjusted indicators can reveal dimensions of adoption that absolute numbers may miss.
The result is a digital-health landscape that is no longer adequately described by a single national leaderboard. India’s digital-health progress in 2026 is becoming a multi-dimensional story of scale, coverage, utilisation, interoperability and system integration.
India’s Digital-Health Foundation at a Glance
Before examining the states, it is important to understand the scale of the national infrastructure on which state-level digital health is now being built.
The figures come from different Government of India and National Health Authority reporting dates and should therefore be read with their respective reporting context.
The distinction between these indicators matters. ABHA creation measures the expansion of the digital identity layer, while HFR and HPR indicate the participation of healthcare facilities and professionals in the national digital ecosystem. ABHA-linked records provide an indicator of digital health-record activity, while Scan and Register offers a more direct measure of patient-facing digital service utilisation.
ABDM's architecture is also designed around interoperability and consent. The government has described ABDM as an ecosystem that facilitates secure exchange of health information between intended stakeholders with patient consent rather than operating as a centralised repository of citizens' health data.
Uttar Pradesh: India’s Scale Leader Moves Towards System Integration
Uttar Pradesh sits at the centre of India’s digital-health scale story. The state had created more than 15.3 crore ABHAs by May 2026, the highest among states. It also emerged as the leading contributor to India's ABHA-linked health records, with more than 15.03 crore records linked at the country's 100-crore milestone.
The larger significance of Uttar Pradesh's progress is that the state is moving beyond digital identity creation. Its eKavach platform has been integrated with ABDM, providing an example of how state-specific digital health systems can connect with the national architecture.
The state’s adoption of citizen-facing digital services provides another indication of this transition. By August 7, Uttar Pradesh had recorded 4.09 crore Scan and Register transactions, making it the second-highest state nationally. This provides an indication of growing use of digital infrastructure at the point where patients enter the healthcare system.
Uttar Pradesh at a glance
- 15.3+ crore ABHAs created by May 2026
- 15.03+ crore ABHA-linked records at the 100-crore national milestone
- 4.09 crore Scan and Register transactions by August 7
- eKavach integrated with ABDM
Andhra Pradesh: High Population Coverage
Andhra Pradesh presents a different model of digital-health progress. The state recorded 98.5% ABHA saturation in the Ministry's May 2026 data, placing it among the strongest-performing large states and Union Territories on population coverage.
It also recorded more than 11.95 crore ABHA-linked health records at the national 100-crore milestone.
The state’s performance becomes even more significant when digital utilisation is considered. Andhra Pradesh had recorded more than 3.38 crore Scan and Register transactions by August 7, placing it third nationally.
The combination of high saturation and high service utilisation illustrates an important dimension of digital-health maturity: moving from ensuring that citizens have digital identities towards incorporating those identities into healthcare interactions.
Bihar: Where Digital Health Reaches the OPD
Bihar's digital-health story is particularly significant because of its performance in Scan and Register. The state had created 6.3 crore ABHAs by May 2026 and recorded more than 7.37 crore ABHA-linked health records at the national 100-crore milestone.
Its strongest indicator in 2026, however, is patient-facing utilisation. Bihar recorded more than 7.30 crore Scan and Register transactions by August 7, the highest among all states and Union Territories.
This is an important shift in the digital-health narrative. Creating an ABHA is an infrastructure milestone, while a completed digital OPD registration provides a stronger indicator of service utilisation.
Nationally, Scan and Register crossed 25 crore OPD registrations by August 7 and was operational across 30,800 healthcare facilities, 756 districts and all 36 States and Union Territories.
What Bihar’s numbers demonstrate
- Digital identity creation
- High-volume digital OPD registration
- Citizen-facing utilisation
- Large-scale implementation across healthcare facilities
Bihar therefore provides an important example of how digital-health infrastructure can become part of everyday healthcare operations.
Rajasthan: Connecting State Platforms to National Infrastructure
Rajasthan's digital-health journey combines scale, population coverage and interoperability. The state had created 7.1 crore ABHAs, with 89.7% ABHA saturation, by May 2026. More than 6.32 crore health records had been linked with ABHAs.
The more strategic development is the integration of Rajasthan's Pregnancy, Child Tracking and Health Services Management System (PCTS) with ABDM. The Ministry has listed PCTS among state and national digital-health platforms integrated with ABDM.
Rajasthan was also honoured at the April 2026 NHA Chintan Shivir in Pune for maximum registration of private healthcare professionals and facilities under ABDM.
This is significant because a national digital-health ecosystem cannot be built through government facilities alone. Private hospitals, clinics and healthcare professionals represent a substantial part of healthcare delivery, making their participation important to building a connected ecosystem.
Maharashtra and West Bengal: Population Scale Remains Important
Maharashtra and West Bengal are among the largest contributors to India's digital-health identity ecosystem. Maharashtra had created approximately 7.1 crore ABHAs, while West Bengal had created 5.9 crore by May 2026.
However, these figures also demonstrate why state-level comparisons need context. Absolute numbers naturally favour larger populations. A more complete comparison therefore needs to combine absolute ABHA creation with saturation, health-record linkage, facility participation and service utilisation.
This multi-metric approach becomes increasingly important as India moves into a more mature phase of digital-health implementation.
Gujarat: Interoperability as the Next Frontier
Gujarat's experience highlights the importance of connecting state-developed platforms with ABDM. The state had contributed more than 4.77 crore ABHA-linked health records at the national 100-crore milestone.
Its TeCHO platform has also been integrated with ABDM, providing another example of state-level digital infrastructure connecting with the national ecosystem.
The importance of such integration goes beyond technology. India's healthcare system operates through a complex combination of central programmes, state health departments, public hospitals, private providers and specialised health platforms. A common interoperability architecture can allow these systems to remain tailored to local requirements while participating in a broader digital-health ecosystem.
Madhya Pradesh: Digital Adoption at the Institutional Level
Madhya Pradesh offers a useful institutional perspective on digital-health adoption. The clearest example is AIIMS Bhopal, which had recorded 29.10 lakh Scan and Register OPD registrations by August 7, 2026, making it the second-highest government facility nationally after AIIMS New Delhi.
The importance of this number lies in its connection to hospital operations. Digital health becomes meaningful when technology is incorporated into everyday workflows used by patients and healthcare workers. High-volume digital registration at a major public hospital therefore provides an example of national digital infrastructure being translated into operational healthcare delivery.
Odisha, Himachal Pradesh and Chhattisgarh: Strong Coverage Across Diverse Geographies
Several states demonstrate the breadth of India's digital-health penetration through high ABHA saturation. Odisha recorded 91.9% saturation, Himachal Pradesh 88.9%, and Chhattisgarh 86.6% in the Ministry's May 2026 assessment.
These figures demonstrate why population coverage is an important complement to absolute ABHA numbers. While states such as Uttar Pradesh lead absolute numbers because of their population size, states with high saturation demonstrate how deeply digital health has penetrated their populations.
Chhattisgarh also featured prominently in the April 2026 NHA Chintan Shivir. It was recognised for timely processing of suspicious claims, while Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh were jointly recognised for best performance among large states in high-trigger efficacy under AB PM-JAY.
Tamil Nadu: Bringing Health Insurance into the Digital-Health Ecosystem
Tamil Nadu illustrates the expanding scope of ABDM through the integration of its Comprehensive Health Insurance Scheme (CMCHIS) with the national digital-health ecosystem.
This is important because healthcare is not limited to clinical interactions. A patient journey can involve registration, consultation, diagnostics, hospitalisation, referral, treatment and insurance claims. Connecting health-financing infrastructure with digital-health architecture can therefore create a broader ecosystem in which clinical and administrative processes can increasingly operate through connected digital workflows.
Karnataka: Digital Referrals and Continuity of Care
Karnataka provides another example of digital infrastructure being used to support healthcare workflows. At the April 2026 NHA Chintan Shivir, the state presented its online referral system for PM-JAY beneficiaries.
Digital referral systems are particularly relevant because healthcare is distributed across multiple levels. Patients may move from primary care to secondary or tertiary facilities, and digital referral infrastructure can support information exchange and continuity across those transitions.

India has called for a more predictable regulatory environment in Brazil to boost exports of pharmaceutical goods, the Commerce Ministry said on Monday (August 31, 2026).
The issue came up for discussion during the eighth meeting of the India-Brazil Trade Monitoring Mechanism (TMM) in Brasilia, Brazil. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agarwal attended the meeting.
In the meeting, progress was made in facilitating market access for Indian pharmaceutical products.
"India emphasised the need for supporting more predictable regulatory pathways and facilitating greater market access," it said.
It added that India can contribute to the availability of affordable, quality medicines and strengthen efforts towards more accessible healthcare.
India and Brazil also agreed for early finalisation of terms of reference for starting negotiations to expand the scope of the existing trade pact between New Delhi and the South American bloc Mercosur.
Mercosur is a trade bloc in Latin America comprising Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, and Paraguay.
The India-Mercosur Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) came into effect on June 1, 2009.
This PTA has limited coverage and contains only 450 tariff lines or products. Both sides are looking at expanding the scope of this pact to a full-fledged agreement.
"The India-Mercosur Preferential Trade Agreement offers considerable scope for expansion and modernisation. With India-Mercosur bilateral trade reaching $20.84 billion in 2025, both sides committed to early finalisation of the Terms of Reference," the Ministry said.
The terms of reference means the agreed framework that sets the scope, objectives, and rules for the negotiations of a trade pact.
Bilateral trade between India and Brazil touched $15.07 billion in 2025-26. The aim is to take the trade to $30 billion by 2030.

agritech-8d01cb77fd.headline: 🎥 Carbon Robotics: $100m+ revenue, new machine and a path to IPO
agritech-8d01cb77fd.fulltext:
Seattle-based Carbon Robotics is aiming to become a publicly traded company as it continues to scale its laser weeding and tractor autonomy business.
The firm, which passed the $100 million revenue mark in the year to March 2026, is also developing an as-yet-unannounced machine—also in the ag robotics field—and says it may raise additional capital to grow its tractor autonomy platform.
While there is potential to move into different industries, the company does not need to diversify beyond agriculture to build a sizable business, says founder and CEO Paul Mikesell, pointing to a market of thousands of laser weeders a year and potentially 30,000–40,000 tractors annually for its autonomy technology.
AgFunderNews (AFN) caught up with Mikesell (PM) at the inaugural Ruggedize ag robotics conference at Reservoir Farms in Salinas to discuss Carbon’s path toward an IPO, the economics of laser weeding, and its autonomy program.
AFN: Can you share an update on your revenues and plans?
PM: Last year, we crossed over $100 million in revenue and we intend to keep scaling from there. It’s our intention to get to the point that we’re an independently publicly traded company, so that would involve going through an IPO. That’s the path that we’re on.
Do we need to have our technology into other things beyond agriculture? I don’t think we need to. There may be a thing we’ll do at some point, particularly on the autonomy side, but it’s not our focus right now. And I think there is plenty of room to make a completely independent, publicly traded company in agriculture. And that’s coming. That’s our goal.
AFN: What’s your addressable market?
PM: The addressable market in terms of number of machines would be thousands of machines a year. And then on the autonomy side, we’re talking probably 30 to 40,000 tractors per year. That’s kind of where we’re going to get to, and so there is a lot of room for us to grow.
We are currently available in about 20 countries around the world, and we’re seeing the most traction in the United States, and then Western Europe, and Australia is pretty strong also. Laser weeders work in all the major growing regions where there’s a lot of vegetables grown.
AFN: How has your offering evolved?
PM: We came out with our second generation G2 LaserWeeder early last year, and we now have multiple sizes of machines. So the smallest would probably be [suitable for farms of] about 50 acres, and then the largest [ones make sense for] farms [that] are hundreds of thousands of acres, and anything in between.
The design of the G2 is more modular, which allows us to fit weeding modules onto a bar, and create something that’s of the appropriate size for the farmer.
There is another machine that we’re building that is independent from that that we haven’t announced yet. But it’s still in the ag space.
AFN: You’re also building new autonomy systems for tractors?
PM: We’re moving pretty quickly in our autonomy systems as well, so we make an autonomous tractor product, and that is where we’re starting to think about raising some [additional] money to continue to expand that product line [following the recent $20 million Series D extension].
It takes an existing tractor and converts it to a completely autonomous system [via advanced perception that combines camera, radar, and lidar inputs with software to create fully autonomous tractor operations]. And so that’s not just for laser weeding, but also for tillage, for cultivation, for irrigation, anything you might want to do.
AFN: Where’s the ROI coming from?
PM: A lot of it is reduced labor, and then a lot of it is if you’re using herbicides today instead of applying herbicides, running a laser weeder has dramatic yield improvements. So 30 or 40, 50% yield improvement in the same field, and that comes from not spraying, which knocks back the crops. And even just not having hand labor in the field will also mean more crops with more vigor because people stepping around and herbicides obviously damage crops.
So dramatic yield improvements [from using laser weeding] have been documented time and time again through university studies and other grower experiences.
The other thing that happens is because you’re not knocking the crops back, they’ll come up two weeks earlier, and so that means you get to market earlier. You have a jump on the market. It means that you’re using less water and less fertilizer also to grow those crops, because again you’re not beating them up as they’re trying to grow.
So a lot of the benefit, a lot of the value comes from yield improvement and getting to market earlier, and higher quality crops overall.
We’ve also been doing things like helping folks go from transplants to direct seeding. Transplanting can cost a lot of money, and if you can direct seed, it’s a much cheaper way to go. But a lot of places they can’t do that because of weed pressure. They wind up having the transplant after the crop is big enough to handle herbicide spray. But instead [with laser weeding], you can just direct seed. We keep the crops clean, and then that saves a lot of money as well.
AFN: How quickly can farmers using the LaserWeeder expect to see a payback?
PM: It should certainly be in less than three years, but our fastest paybacks are less than a year.
AFN: Does the hefty price tag put customers off?
PM: The machines were so successful that we started getting more and more customers and eventually, the banks were coming to us saying, Okay, how do we help finance these things because we understand what this machine is, we see the residual value and we understand there’s a resale value. We’d like to help these farmers get access to them. So once you hit that point, it becomes easier.
Now some of these banks are doing things like writing an operating lease for LaserWeeders. With an operating lease, you don’t have to put capital up front; you just pay a certain amount every month, and then as long as you’re making more money than that off the benefits from the LaserWeeder, you’re cash positive immediately.
AFN: Talk a bit about what you’ve learned about the business model that works for you…
PM: Going through a dealership to do something like service and support puts you one step removed from your customer. And we just didn’t like that model at all. We want to feel like if the customer has something wrong, something they need, if a farmer or a grower has something they need to understand better, we want them to communicate with us directly, rather than a sort of hands-off approach.
AFN: Doesn’t selling direct restrict the speed with which you can grow in international markets?
PM: In international markets, we do the same [direct sales] model. So everywhere that we have LaserWeeders, we have our own sales force and we have our own support team, and those people are on the ground in the region.
A lot of them came from a farming background in the region, so they know the crops, they know the soil type, they know the farmers, and so that works really well for us.

agritech-a8ea49cb0f.headline: India’s Shift to Grain-Based Ethanol, Food and Water Security Concerns
agritech-a8ea49cb0f.fulltext:
India’s ethanol programme is undergoing a major structural shift. Originally designed to support the sugar industry and sugarcane farmers, it is increasingly dependent on grain-based ethanol, particularly from maize and rice.
This shift has helped India move towards E20, but also raises concerns over food security, water stress and sustainable feedstock availability, especially as sugar stocks tighten, maize faces climate risks and FCI rice is increasingly used for ethanol.
Why Was the Ethanol Programme Introduced?
The Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme was initially intended to address problems in the sugar sector while strengthening India’s energy security.
- Support sugar mills: Ethanol provides sugar mills with an additional revenue stream when sugar production exceeds market demand.
- Ensure timely cane payments: Additional ethanol revenue improves mill liquidity and helps sugar mills make timely payments to sugarcane farmers.
- Manage sugar surplus: Diverting part of sugarcane towards ethanol reduces surplus sugar production and helps stabilise the sugar market.
- Reduce crude oil dependence: Blending domestic ethanol with petrol reduces the requirement for imported petroleum and strengthens energy security.
- Create an agricultural market: The programme has also created additional demand for crops such as maize, which is traditionally used for poultry and livestock feed.
How Did India Shift to Grain-Based Ethanol?
India’s shift to grain-based ethanol took place as the government expanded the feedstock base and ethanol demand increased.
- Until 2017-18, ethanol supplied to oil marketing companies came almost entirely from C-heavy molasses, a by-product of sugar production.
- From 2018-19, mills were encouraged to use B-heavy molasses and sugarcane juice/syrup for ethanol, which increased the quantity of sugarcane diverted towards fuel.
- Grains initially entered as an off-season feedstock, with sugar mills using maize and rice during May-October, when sugarcane was not available for crushing.
- Standalone grain distilleries later expanded, allowing ethanol production from maize and rice throughout the year rather than depending on the sugarcane crushing season.
- Rising ethanol blending targets increased demand for grain-based ethanol, while high sugar prices and lower sugar stocks reduced the scope for diverting sugarcane juice and B-heavy molasses.
- The result was a sharp reversal in the feedstock mix. Sugarcane-based feedstock supplied over 83% of ethanol in 2021-22, but grains accounted for 59.7% in 2023-24 and 72.5% of allocated ethanol for the supply year ending October 2026.
Thus, grains have evolved from a supplementary off-season feedstock into the mainstay of India’s ethanol programme.
What Are the Concerns with the Shift to Grain-Based Ethanol?
The growing dependence on grains for ethanol is creating new pressures on food security, agricultural markets, water resources and sustainable feedstock availability.
- Using food grains for ethanol can intensify the food-versus-fuel trade-off, as maize and rice are also required for food consumption, poultry and livestock feed.
- Rising ethanol demand can put pressure on maize supplies, as it has created a major new source of demand alongside poultry and livestock feed. Wholesale maize prices rose from around ₹13.8-17.8 per kg in 2021 to ₹22.1–24.5 per kg in 2024.
- Greater reliance on ethanol can increase dependence on Food Corporation of India rice, particularly if maize supplies tighten and sugarcane-based ethanol remains constrained.
- Diversion of Food Corporation of India rice raises questions about its opportunity cost, as rice used for ethanol cannot simultaneously serve as food, animal feed or a buffer against future shortages. Food Corporation of India rice was supplied to distilleries at around ₹23.2 per kg, compared with about ₹40 per kg for normal rice and ₹30 per kg for broken rice in the retail market.
- Greater dependence on rice can worsen water stress, as rice is a water-intensive crop and rising demand for it as an ethanol feedstock can reinforce water-intensive cropping patterns.
- Dependence on a few feedstocks increases climate vulnerability, as weather shocks affecting maize or other major crops can directly affect ethanol availability.
- Rapid expansion of ethanol capacity can increase pressure on agricultural feedstocks, with capacity nearing 2,000 crore litres against annual offtake of around 1,050 crore litres by oil marketing companies.
- Ethanol production can also reduce the sugar available for consumption, because some sugarcane is diverted towards ethanol instead of being converted into sugar. This diversion was 2.2 million tonnes in 2020-21, 4.3 million tonnes in 2022-23 and 3 million tonnes in 2025-26, showing that ethanol production can significantly affect the sugar supply.
Thus, the shift to grain-based ethanol may reduce dependence on sugarcane, but it also transfers pressure towards India’s food, feed and water resources.
What Is the Central Policy Dilemma?
The issue now is not whether ethanol blending should be promoted, but how rapidly it should be expanded without creating unsustainable pressure on agricultural resources.
- Achieving E20 requires around 1,050 crore litres of ethanol annually, creating substantial and sustained demand for feedstocks.
- The government has already notified standards for E22, E25, E27 and E30, indicating the possibility of progressively higher blending in the future.
- Higher blending targets should be linked to the availability of sustainable feedstocks, rather than being driven primarily by installed distillery capacity.
- The benefits of reducing fossil-fuel dependence must be balanced against the competing demands on food grains, land and water.
- Consolidating E20 while developing alternative feedstocks and second-generation ethanol could reduce pressure to divert increasing quantities of food grains.
The central challenge is to expand ethanol blending without compromising India’s food and water security.
What Should India Do?
India needs to move from a target-driven ethanol strategy towards a diversified and resource-efficient feedstock strategy.
- Reduce excessive dependence on FCI rice: Public food stocks should be diverted to ethanol only when they are genuinely surplus after accounting for food-security requirements.
- Use maize within sustainable limits: Rising ethanol demand should not undermine maize availability for poultry, livestock feed and other essential uses.
- Promote bajra and jowar: Millets offer alternative feedstocks, with their grains containing around 58-62% recoverable starch and yielding approximately 380-400 litres of ethanol per tonne.
- Link ethanol with crop diversification: Encouraging less water-intensive feedstocks can reduce pressure on rice and sugarcane while creating additional markets for millet farmers.
- Promote second-generation ethanol: Agricultural residues and other lignocellulosic biomass can produce ethanol without directly competing with food crops.
- Adopt region-specific feedstock planning: Ethanol production should reflect local water availability, agro-climatic conditions and crop suitability rather than relying uniformly on rice, maize or sugarcane.
- Avoid capacity-driven blending targets: Expansion of distillery capacity should not by itself become a reason for continuously raising blending targets.
- Increase blending gradually: The pace of blending should remain aligned with the availability of sustainable and diversified feedstocks.
- Reassess the pace of expansion: Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran has suggested returning to E10, highlighting the need to examine whether higher blending should be pursued at the current pace.
Conclusion
India’s shift to grain-based ethanol has strengthened energy security but has also created new pressures on food grains, water and agricultural resources. The way forward is to diversify feedstocks, expand 2G ethanol and align blending targets with sustainable resource availability.

indian-startups-e0ace89ac7.headline: Semicon 2.0 sets investment thresholds, offers 40% fab subsidy, Rs 15 crore startup funding
indian-startups-e0ace89ac7.fulltext:
The notification follows the Union Cabinet's approval of a Rs 1.27 lakh crore outlay for India Semiconductor Mission 2.0. The programme covers six pillars and 10 categories across the semiconductor value chain.
                    
                                        
                    
                    
                    New Delhi, August 31: Companies seeking to participate in the government's Semicon 2.0 programme will have to meet specific technology, investment, revenue and capacity requirements, depending on the segment of the semiconductor value chain, according to the scheme notified by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on Monday.
For strategic semiconductor design, companies must be incorporated and headquartered in India, have a significant operational and manpower presence in the country and be owned and controlled by Indian citizens. They can apply either independently or in partnership with global companies, research organisations and academic institutions.
For commercial semiconductor design, companies must also be incorporated and headquartered in India and have a significant presence in the country. They must be owned and controlled by Indian citizens or Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs).
Eligible startups and MSMEs can get milestone-linked seed funding of 50 per cent of the project cost or Rs 15 crore, whichever is lower. Companies backed by venture capital or private equity can also receive equity co-investment.
The scheme also offers royalty financing to larger eligible companies. Under this arrangement, beneficiaries will pay 5 per cent of the net revenue generated from the product or technology until 1.5 times the government support is recovered.
For newly launched semiconductor intellectual property (IP), chips and system-on-chips (SoCs), eligible applicants can get a 9 per cent reimbursement on net sales for five years. The support will be capped at Rs 30 crore per application and Rs 120 crore per company, including group companies.
For equipment R&D facilities, the minimum investment requirement is Rs 300 crore and minimum revenue requirement is Rs 120 crore. Raw-material facilities will need a minimum investment of Rs 50 crore and revenue of Rs 20 crore, while test and characterisation facilities will require Rs 100 crore investment and Rs 40 crore revenue.
Equipment and component manufacturing facilities will require a minimum investment of Rs 300 crore and revenue of Rs 120 crore. These segments will be eligible for government support of 30 per cent of eligible capital expenditure.
Equipment and component manufacturers can also receive a production-linked incentive (PLI) ranging from 10 per cent to 2 per cent of the value of components sourced from domestic manufacturers for five years from FY2028-29. The overall support will be capped at 50 per cent of eligible capital expenditure.
The highest eligibility requirements have been set for silicon wafer fabrication plants. Projects must use 300-mm wafers, have a capacity of at least 40,000 wafer starts per month and use production-grade licensed technology. They must invest at least Rs 20,000 crore and have minimum revenue of Rs 7,500 crore in at least one of the previous three financial years.
The government will provide 40 per cent of eligible capital expenditure for such projects on a pari-passu basis.
For compound semiconductor, photonics, sensor/MEMS and discrete semiconductor fabs, the minimum investment requirement is Rs 500 crore, revenue requirement is Rs 200 crore and capacity must be at least 500 wafer starts per month. These projects will receive 35 per cent support on eligible capital expenditure.
For ATMP/OSAT facilities, advanced packaging projects will require a minimum investment of Rs 1,000 crore and revenue of Rs 200 crore and will receive 35 per cent capex support. Legacy packaging projects with the same investment and revenue requirements will receive 25 per cent support.
The scheme also provides government support of up to 75 per cent of project cost for advanced semiconductor research and development, covering eligible capital and operating expenditure.
The India Semiconductor Mission will act as the nodal agency and assess applications based on technical and financial parameters, including process technology, project implementation capability, operational capability and off-take.
The scheme will initially remain open for applications for three years. (ANI)

indian-startups-d33bea50fc.headline: Indian Startup IPO Tracker 2026
indian-startups-d33bea50fc.fulltext: Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, ten new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, Klassroom, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Thirty two startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 24 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Sarvam AI Co-founder Vivek Raghavan named among TIME’s top 100 AI leaders
Raghavan launched Sarvam AI with co-founder Pratyush Kumar in 2023, aiming to create India’s own sovereign LLM ecosystem that could compete with global AI players.
The Co-founder of Sarvam AI, Vivek Raghavan, has been named to TIME magazine’s TIME100 AI 2026 list of the world’s 100 most influential leaders in artificial intelligence.
In a post on X, Bengaluru-based Sarvam AI said the recognition reflects Raghavan’s decades of work building technology infrastructure to make technology more useful and accessible.
“We’re proud to share that @vivekrag has been named in TIME100 AI 2026,
@TIME magazine’s list of the world’s 100 most influential leaders in AI. This recognition reflects his work over the decades building the rails that make technology more useful and accessible to people (sic),” the official handle of Sarvam said on X.
Raghavan was involved in building Aadhaar, a biometric identification system that consists of a 12-digit unique identity number which residents of India can obtain voluntarily based on their place of residence, biometric and demographic data.
Raghavan launched Sarvam AI with co-founder Pratyush Kumar in 2023, aiming to create multilingual Indian AI models that could compete with global AI players in the West.
In February, Sarvam launched Sarvam Vision, its frontier vision language model. The company said the model can scan and extract text from documents in 22 Indian languages and English with a higher word accuracy rate than Gemini and ChatGPT.
In March, the homegrown AI startup released Sarvam 30B and 105B, two open-source, open-weight models capable of advanced reasoning, coding, mathematics and other high-level tasks. The models could enable Indian developers and companies to build their own applications.
In August, Nvidia became a strategic investor in Sarvam AI, joining a roughly $75 million Series B funding round that values the company at about $1.5 billion.
Importance of AI sovereignty
Earlier, Raghavan has been vocal about the importance of AI sovereignty in the subcontinent and of building a homegrown, Indian-language AI stack rather than relying on foreign technology companies.
He has said India is a large market for several US technology companies, some of which provide their services for free.
“But the question is, what is really free?” Raghavan said in an interview with Indian news outlet Bharatvaarta.
He has described Indians as “exporting our data and importing intelligence”, comparing it with India exporting cotton and importing cloth a century ago.

ABLE Labs, a South Korean startup specializing in laboratory automation robotics, has raised approximately $8.7 million (KRW 12.1 billion) in Series A funding, the company announced on August 31.
The round was led by Innopolis Partners and joined by Industrial Bank of Korea, Capstone Partners, Horizon Investment, Magna Investment, Futureplay, and NAU IB Capital.
ABLE Labs plans to expand its business from liquid-handling robotics to self-driving laboratories and build infrastructure for generating experimental data to train AI models.
The company has secured new quality-analysis automation projects across four industries beyond biotechnology: semiconductors, chemicals, cosmetics, and secondary batteries. Revenue in 2025 reached KRW 1.29 billion, up 113 percent year over year, while order intake in the first half of 2026 already exceeded twice the prior year’s full-year revenue.
ABLE Labs has deployed laboratory automation solutions at KAIST, Pusan National University, and the Korea Research Institute of Chemical Technology. The company is jointly developing an organoid-based drug evaluation platform with Johns Hopkins University in the United States. To date, the startup has carried out eight national R&D projects and secured over KRW 10 billion in government research funding over five years.
ABLE Labs is currently conducting a proof-of-concept project with a major U.S. pharmaceutical company and has completed product delivery to its first customer in Singapore.
In the South Korean lab-automation and advanced-materials market, deep-tech startups have been raising capital to scale hardware and AI-enabled R&D platforms. LABINCUBE raised $9.9M in Series B to commercialize Metal-Organic Framework materials for chemical and energy applications, while QUAD closed a pre-Series A round to bring superconducting single-photon detectors to semiconductor inspection and quantum computing markets.

india-deep-tech-e44d170539.headline: Diffraqtion raises funding for quantum imaging technology
india-deep-tech-e44d170539.fulltext:
WASHINGTON — A startup has raised $10 million from investors that include Lockheed Martin and Sumitomo to advance technology for space cameras that promises to resolve details not possible with conventional systems.
Diffraqtion announced Aug. 31 it closed a pre-seed round involving Lockheed Martin Ventures and Presidio Ventures, the venture arm of Sumitomo Corp., among other investors. The company said strong interest led it to cap the pre-seed round.
The company, based in Somerville, Massachusetts, and spun out of work done at the University of Maryland and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, is developing quantum cameras it says can get around the resolution limit of conventional cameras, known as the diffraction limit. That limit is a function of the wavelength of light and the diameter of the imager: To improve the resolution, one must use shorter wavelengths or larger apertures.
The diffraction limit “is just a limit that is imposed by the technique of direct imaging,” said Johannes Galatsanos, co-founder and chief executive of Diffraqtion, in an interview. “For a very long time, we have thought this is the limit.”
The company says it has developed a way to extract quantum information from photons using an approach called modal imaging. Another company co-founder, Saikat Guha, has worked on this technology for more than a decade.
“Instead of looking at intensity of the light, you’re looking at the shapes or the modes,” Galatsanos said. “When you’re looking at the shape of the light that comes to you, you can extract properties about the object that sent that light.”
An example he gave was taking an image of a satellite. While a conventional image might show only a blur, the company’s quantum imaging techniques could reveal the shape or orientation of the spacecraft. Simulations indicate the technology could resolve features 20 times smaller than conventional cameras.
The company has tested the technology in the lab and, in January, announced a $1.5 million Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency Small Business Innovation Research contract to test the technology on ground-based telescopes.
Galatsanos said the pre-seed round will allow the company to develop its first full camera system with “much higher” performance than the one used in the lab and test it on telescopes. The company is also proposing to fly a version of the camera as a hosted payload on a spacecraft in 2028, but he said the company will need to raise additional funding for that milestone.
Initial interest in Diffraqtion’s technology is its use in space domain awareness. “You can say that this is a certain type of a satellite, or this is a satellite in a certain orientation, or this is a satellite versus debris or something else,” he said.
A downside of this technology, he acknowledged, is that while the sensor can return information about the shape of the object, it does not provide an image. The technology is best used in a “sensor fusion” approach that combines the shape information it provides with data from other cameras that can produce conventional images. “We always foresee this to be used in tandem with other sensors,” he said.
Since receiving the DARPA award in January, Diffraqtion has received inquiries about its sensor technology in a wide range of applications. That is one reason Sumitomo’s venture arm invested in the company. “They see the wider applications of this across robotics, drones and industrial inspections,” he said.
“What drew us to Diffraqtion is that the same physics advantage applies whether the camera is observing the sky or the Earth, or guiding a physical system,” said Ross Leav, senior vice president at Presidio Ventures, in a statement. “We see significant opportunity to bring this capability to industrial and commercial markets globally.”
“We invest in technologies with the potential to shape future mission capabilities,” said Chris Moran, vice president and general manager of Lockheed Martin Ventures, in the statement. “This team’s rapid progress from laboratory development toward flight demonstration is particularly promising.”

india-deep-tech-fbd1a9c7e2.headline: Reframe Systems raises $40M to scale its robotic microfactories for home building
india-deep-tech-fbd1a9c7e2.fulltext:
Reframe Systems, a robotics company using physical AI to industrialize home construction, today announced said it has raised $40 million. The company said the funding will help it scale its microfactory network across North America.
Currently, the U.S. is short 4.5 million homes. Reframe said this problem stems from the construction industry’s fragmented nature. Most houses are build by hand, involving 25 or more subcontractors that are drawing on a shrinking pool of skilled trades.
Reframe hopes to address this issue by building a network of automated microfactories near communities where homes are needed. This allows the company to adapt production to different zoning requirements, climate conditions, and architectural styles.
“The housing shortage is an abstraction until you’re the person who can’t find a home in the community you want to live in,” said Vikas Enti, co-founder and CEO of Reframe Systems. “Developers are demanding faster, energy-efficient, climate-resilient homes and we are answering that demand. With our technology, we’re able to deliver infill housing, such as a triple-decker in Somerville in 180 days and help families in Altadena rebuild wildfire-resilient bungalows in months instead of years.”
“With our model, every home we deliver makes the next one faster and cheaper to build, because our software, robotics and network learn from each deployment,” he said. “That demand is why we’re expanding, and why we’re now targeting one million homes by 2040, five years ahead of schedule.”
Reframe to open a new microfactory in October
Reframe plans to expand its production capacity by opening FAB1, a new microfactory in Billerica, Mass. The company plans to begin operations at FAB1 on Oct. 5. This means it will achieve full factory readiness in just 70 days from receiving the keys. The factory will use less than $5 million in equipment. Reframe designed FAB1 to produce up to 500 multifamily units or 250 single-family homes annually.
So far, Reframe has completed 10 homes which range from accessory dwelling units (ADUs) to triple-decker apartments. Eight of these homes are already occupied.
Over the next year, Reframe plans to deliver 114 more units. The company aims to build 1 million homes worldwide by 2040.
At Adams Circle in Devens, Mass., Reframe is finishing 12 units for delivery. It has a five-story apartment building in Roxbury and a development in Thornton, N.H., next in the factory pipeline to build.
In Altadena, Calif., Reframe is completing a wildfire-resilient bungalow and an ADU to help a family rebuild after the fires.
“After the fires, we were being told that a traditional construction rebuild could take years and could cost far more than we could afford. Reframe streamlined the process, secured the permits, coordinated with a contractor, and is completing our new wildfire-resilient home in months at a cost that worked for our family,” said Jonathan Talbot and Marisol Talbot, homeowners of the Altadena bungalow. “That difference in timeline, cost, and security allowed us to move forward with confidence.”
More about the funding round
Energy Impact Partners (EIP) led the funding round. It also included investments from Counterpart Ventures, E12 Ventures, Global Brain, Thin Line Capital, Up Partners and LACI Impact Fund. The company saw support from existing investors Eclipse, VoLo Earth, Cubit Capital, RA Capital Management (Planetary Health), MassMutual Catalyst and Nor’easter.
The additional capital positions Reframe to accelerate home delivery in New England and deploy additional microfactory capacity across North America. It aims to bring its robotics-enabled homebuilding to the communities that need it most.
Reframe Systems was founded by former Amazon Robotics leaders Vikas Enti, Felipe Polido, and Aaron Small in 2022. At Amazon, the three helped to scale automation systems and deploy more than 500,000 robots across Amazon’s global fulfillment network.

global-economics-e22c34e8bc.fulltext:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has urged Russia to end the Ukraine war and for a cessation of hostilities during his meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit on Monday.
"India supports all peace efforts in this area [Ukraine war], and we will continue to do so," Modi said, adding that "we must move from endless war to the end of war, to the cessation of hostilities."
"Every day that the war continues, humanity takes a step backwards," Modi said.
On Monday, Russia's Defense Ministry said it is planning "massive strikes" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, days after launching a devastating attack on an ammunition warehouse, amplifying fears of another winter assault.
Russian strike on the warehouse is among its deadliest attacks in Ukraine so far, with a death toll of 38. Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure during winter pose Kyiv's toughest challenge of the war yet, as per officials and national security experts.
Meanwhile, later this month, the U.S. House is expected to pass a bill honoring Lindsey Graham that would impose up to 100% tariffs on countries that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas, including China and India.
Russia is India's largest crude supplier, accounting for more than 50% of the country's oil imports in June and July and nearly 43% till August 24. Between April and July, Russian exports to India rose to over $34 billion, up nearly 60% from last year, as per India's latest trade data.
During the meeting with Modi, Putin commended the growth in bilateral trade between the two countries but added that "last year saw a slight decline."
U.S. President Donald Trump imposed punitive tariffs of 25% on India in August 2025 for its energy trade with Russia, taking the total levy on Indian exports to the U.S. to 50%.
While the tariffs on India have been reduced to 18% earlier this year, the U.S. has been keen to increase the supply of Venezuelan crude to India to replace the Russian barrels.

other-interests-eb110d1ece.headline: Growing Indigenous food trees in East Africa fights malnutrition and biodiversity loss
other-interests-eb110d1ece.fulltext:
- In East Africa, many communities are experiencing both malnutrition and a loss of biodiversity due to deforestation.
- Despite this, tree-planting programs frequently focus on fast-growing, non-native species that can be utilized for timber, rather than food-bearing native trees.
- A recent workshop in Malawi provided landscape restoration workers with a tree-planting guide for local species and gathered information about what organizations and communities need to plant these trees more frequently.
- These findings are summarized in a new paper.
When the sugary-sweet masuku plum is in season in Malawi, locals go wild over it. “They will eat it while traveling, in the bath, on the streets … they just eat,” said Richard Swirah, an agroecologist with the Malawi chapter of the organization WeForest.
Swirah has seen firsthand that native fruits like the masuku (Uapaca kirkiana) are in high demand in local markets — ”they sell like hot cakes,” he told Mongabay during a Zoom interview — but the supply is incredibly scarce. Owing to high levels of deforestation, native food-bearing trees such as the Masuku are becoming increasingly rare in Malawi and across East Africa.
Recent work hopes to reverse this trend. Swirah is one of 40 people who participated in workshops earlier this year to share knowledge and questions about the use of Indigenous food trees in landscape restoration work, an area where they have so far been underutilized. Organized by University of Copenhagen postdoctoral fellow Emilie Vansant, the workshops identified the main challenges to integrating Indigenous food trees into the East African landscape, where tree-planting initiatives often focus on fast-growing, non-native timber species. These findings are summarized in a paper published in June.
“Something important to highlight is that this work is not advocating for all introduced or all Indigenous trees, but for an integration — broadening the scope a bit to include these Indigenous tree species, because of their benefits for diets and biodiversity,” Vansant told Mongabay over Zoom.
Vansant’s interest in Indigenous food trees came from her Ph.D. work, in which she surveyed households in Malawi to find out how forests and backyard trees influenced people’s diets. She found that women who were supplementing their diets with food from these trees had higher levels of important nutrients, such as folate, zinc and vitamin A. She also knew these same trees promoted better conditions for diverse native plants and animals.
These findings sparked a realization for Vansant: Planting more of these trees might be a solution for both chronic malnutrition and biodiversity loss from deforestation.
But Vansant said that when she and her team spoke with farmers, they said they lacked information on how to plant more native trees; indeed, the only resource she could find was a tree-planting guide for Africa as a whole, published in 1993 by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the U.N. (FAO).
In response, after concluding her Ph.D., Vansant worked with collaborators from Copenhagen and Malawi, including Malawian foresters, botanists and agroecologists, to create an illustrated guide to planting, caring for and collecting seeds from edible tree species native to East Africa. The vast majority of these are fruit trees like the masuku plum, though many have multiple edible or medicinal products, such as the African custard-apple (Annona senegalensis), which bears edible fruit, flowers that can be used as a spice and leaves that can be cooked like a vegetable. Another species included was the marula (Sclerocarya birrea) which has high-protein seeds inside its edible fruits that can be ground into flour or pressed into oil.
Vansant’s team presented this guide in the two workshops, using it as a jumping-off point for discussions about what practitioners needed to make better use of these trees.
Vansant was unsurprised to find that the link between public health and ecological health, which she said are usually separated fields of study in Europe and the U.S., was apparent to Malawians.
“When I did my PhD research, visiting households and doing these dietary surveys, I was just blown away by the amount of species I had never heard of, but also the uses that farmers had for each species,” she said. “These farmers had an intimate knowledge of their direct environment, but also this intersection between ecological health and human health. It’s a given: that’s something they didn’t have to buy into.”
Challenges to growing Indigenous food trees
The workshops also identified three areas that practitioners agreed lacked resources, creating an obstacle to using these trees in their work. One of the biggest challenges came with simply helping these trees survive: Their seeds tend to have a very narrow window of time during which they’re viable and the trees themselves only survive in a limited set of environmental conditions. The new tree-planting guide serves as a start, but practitioners are still lacking much species-specific information, Vansant said.
Additionally, the practitioners shared that there are few commercial outlets where they can sell the products of these native trees, which lowers their financial value compared to more marketable products such as non-native timber. This last factor is an important one for many farmers. Indigenous trees’ specific needs and the fact that they grow much slower make them more risky than commercial species bred for hardiness and productivity.
“I don’t see people saying no to Indigenous food trees on principle, but when time and money is involved, that’s a major challenge,” Vansant said. “Creating market opportunities is one way to address the longer time and labor prospects associated with these species.”
Community-controlled income
Experts caution that these market opportunities should be created carefully, however. Nils McCune, an agroecology researcher at the University of Vermont not involved with Vansant’s study, has worked with community-based agroecology projects all over the world.
Two projects he has worked with were in Ghana and included processing facilities for locally grown baobab (Adansonia digitata), a native fruit that has recently grown in popularity around the world. The facilities have been successful in creating valuable products from every part of the baobab, but most importantly, McCune said, the entire process is managed by the community. The money generated returns to that community as profit for farmers, salaries for working in the processing facility and access to credit and loans.
“The idea of generating an economic surplus, or generating an income stream, should somehow be tied to community control,” McCune told Mongabay over a Zoom call. This helps guard against outside interests which can warp well-meaning initiatives into focusing on only the final product, rather than the community — plant, animal and human — that it supports, he said: “Most economic textbooks only see one product looking at a coffee farm, for example, not the migratory birds and insects and other stuff that rely on it.”
Vansant said most communities in Malawi aren’t yet at the level of figuring out this structure, though she has heard of promising first steps taken by workshop participants already. One government botanist and forester let her know that he had been using the tree-planting guide to hold workshops on how to collect, process and store Indigenous seeds. Josie Redmonds, a workshop participant who runs the community nonprofit ButterflySpace, has been integrating the trees from the guide into tree-mapping lessons for local teachers, so that children in Malawi will grow up knowing their native species.
At WeForest, one of Swirah’s priorities is reforesting areas that have been cleared, which includes establishing agroforestry patches alongside fast-growing trees. Swirah and his team were working to integrate more Indigenous species before the workshops, including training local communities on how to collect and save local seeds. The tree-planting guide created by Vansant’s team has provided his team with resources to tailor their techniques to better fit different species. Since the workshop, he’s also been focused on how WeForest can use these trees to create opportunities for the communities it works with.
“What I am really looking for is funds to put much more effort into this, and upscale the promotion of indigenous trees on a larger scale, so that the communities can be self-reliant and benefit from the sales of these fruit trees,” Swirah said. Already, he sees opportunities in selling native fruits to local wineries and breweries and is keenly aware that the time to act for the environment and local communities is now.
“If we can start doing this now, we can do much more now from where we are,” he said. “We will not stop: it is in my heart to be promoted.”

opportunities-6804bc5e6c.headline: GaiaLink Climate Communication Fellowship 2026: Applications Open for Cohort 2
opportunities-6804bc5e6c.fulltext:
GaiaLink has opened applications for the Climate Communication Fellowship – Cohort 2, a six-week immersive development programme designed for young Indian changemakers aged 18–35 who want to strengthen their ability to communicate climate issues and inspire meaningful action.
The fellowship is built around a central question: if climate change affects everyone, why does it often feel disconnected from everyday conversations? GaiaLink’s programme seeks to address this communication gap by combining climate science, behavioural psychology, storytelling, systems thinking and practical campaign development.
Applications for Cohort 2 are open until 2 September 2026.
About the Climate Communication Fellowship
Launched in 2024, GaiaLink’s Climate Communication Fellowship was developed from insights gathered through workshops and extensive conversations on climate and sustainability. The programme recognizes that limited climate action is not necessarily caused by a lack of information. Instead, the challenge often lies in making climate issues relatable, emotionally meaningful and connected to people’s everyday experiences.
The fellowship therefore trains participants to question intentions, decode narratives, understand audience behaviour and develop communication strategies that can turn climate concern into action.
The programme is particularly suited to young professionals, students, communicators, researchers and sustainability enthusiasts who want to become more effective climate storytellers.
Fellowship Format and Duration
The Climate Communication Fellowship is delivered through a hybrid format across Delhi-NCR. Participants should expect to dedicate approximately 6–10 hours per week to the programme.
Weekday evenings feature interactive online workshops, discussions and learning sessions, while weekends include practical field experiences across Delhi-NCR. These may involve visits to urban forests, circular economy initiatives and other sustainability-focused locations.
The programme emphasizes collaboration rather than competition, allowing fellows to co-create campaigns, exchange ideas and develop relationships with peers, mentors and professionals working across the climate sector.
What Participants Will Learn
Throughout the six-week programme, fellows will develop practical and conceptual skills covering climate science, communication and behavioural change.
Key learning areas include:
• Understanding the science of climate change from both global and Indian perspectives
• Exploring the psychology and behavioural factors behind climate inaction
• Understanding cognitive biases, emotional triggers and narrative framing
• Identifying and decoding corporate greenwashing
• Examining government climate policy and India’s Nationally Determined Contributions
• Translating research into accessible and engaging content
• Developing communication strategies for different audiences and platforms
• Creating emotionally resonant climate stories and campaigns
• Designing and presenting a complete climate communication strategy
Six-Week Curriculum
The curriculum progresses from foundational knowledge to practical campaign development.
Week 1 – The Basics: Participants explore climate science and the fundamentals of climate communication, including why facts alone may not drive behavioural change.
Week 2 – India’s Climate Reality: The module examines India-specific climate impacts, regional vulnerabilities and the importance of connecting global climate issues to local realities.
Week 3 – Psychology, Behaviour & Narrative Framing: Fellows investigate cognitive biases, denial, emotional triggers and the role of narratives in influencing climate engagement.
Week 4 – Systemic Overview & Narrative Decode: Participants examine government climate policy, India’s NDC commitments and corporate greenwashing.
Week 5 – Format & Distribution: Fellows learn how to transform research into effective content, select appropriate formats and develop distribution strategies.
Week 6 – Strategy & Pitch: Participants bring their learning together by developing and presenting a complete climate communication campaign strategy.
Who Should Apply?
The fellowship welcomes young Indians aged 18–35 from diverse academic and professional backgrounds.
It is particularly relevant to students and young professionals working or studying in areas such as communication, environmental studies, climate policy, psychology, design and media.
The programme also welcomes curious individuals who want to communicate climate issues with greater empathy and clarity, as well as storytellers interested in connecting climate action with human experiences and systems thinking.
Programme Fee and Key Dates
The fellowship carries a programme fee of INR 6,999.
Important dates include:
• Applications close: 2 September 2026
• Programme induction: 5 September 2026
• Programme completion: 17 October 2026
The fellowship is a six-week intensive programme combining online learning, field visits, workshops, campaign development and networking.
Why the Fellowship Stands Out
GaiaLink describes the programme as human-first and science-rooted, combining environmental science with behavioural psychology, empathy mapping and systems thinking.
Its approach is also deeply local while maintaining a connection to broader global climate frameworks. Rather than relying solely on lectures, participants learn through workshops, field experiences, storytelling exercises and campaign design.
Fellows also become part of a growing network involving mentors, researchers, speakers and grassroots sustainability leaders.
Application Information
Interested applicants can apply for GaiaLink’s Climate Communication Fellowship Cohort 2 before the 2 September 2026 deadline. The opportunity provides participants with an intensive platform to develop climate communication skills, gain practical experience and connect with others working toward a more sustainable future.
The programme is particularly valuable for individuals who believe that effective climate action requires more than communicating scientific facts—it requires creating stories, connections and conversations that motivate people to act.
Applications can be submitted through the official GaiaLink application form.

The fellowship is available only to registered full-time PhD candidates enrolled in:
